```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R")
library(bayesmokken)
```

```{r fit, include = FALSE}
data(srs)
fit <- bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 2000, seed = 1)
iv <- bm_interval(fit)
```

This vignette collects the reasons to believe a number this package produced:
what makes it recomputable, what would tell you it is unreliable, and what
evidence stands behind the method. It closes with the limits.

## The RNG contract

Stochastic results are reproducible only if the randomness is pinned. Three
guarantees hold here.

**A seed is required and recorded.** There is no unseeded path.

```{r seed}
bm_provenance(fit)[c("seed", "rng_kind", "total_draws")]
```

**The seed must be an integer.** Version 0.0.0.9001 fixed a defect where a
fractional seed was silently truncated, so `1.1` and `1L` produced identical
streams while the documentation promised an integer. It now refuses:

```{r fractional, error = TRUE}
bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 200, seed = 1.5)
```

**Binary numeric draws are batch-invariant to within floating-point
accumulation order.** With a fixed seed, changing the binary engine's batch
size does not change which respondent weights are drawn, so the pair, item and
scale draws agree. The agreement is bit-for-bit on most platforms, but the
batch partition does change the order in which the weighted sums accumulate,
and floating-point addition is not associative. The check below therefore
reports the largest disagreement rather than demanding bit equality: a real
batching defect would move the draws by far more than the last bits of a
double.

Bit-for-bit reproducibility is guaranteed for the case that matters — the same
seed, the same batch size, the same platform.

**Metamorphic/invariant check — change the batch partition while holding seed
and requested draws fixed.**

```{r verify-batch}
a <- bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 1000, seed = 7, batch_size = 250, warn = FALSE)
b <- bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 1000, seed = 7, batch_size = 97,  warn = FALSE)

batch_check <- data.frame(
  level = c("scale", "item", "pair"),
  bit_identical = c(
    identical(a$draws$scale, b$draws$scale),
    identical(a$draws$item,  b$draws$item),
    identical(a$draws$pair,  b$draws$pair)
  ),
  max_abs_difference = c(
    max(abs(as.numeric(a$draws$scale) - as.numeric(b$draws$scale))),
    max(abs(as.numeric(a$draws$item)  - as.numeric(b$draws$item))),
    max(abs(as.numeric(a$draws$pair)  - as.numeric(b$draws$pair)))
  )
)
batch_check

# Far tighter than any batching defect could hide under, far looser than
# demanding that two accumulation orders round identically.
stopifnot(all(batch_check$max_abs_difference < 1e-12))
```

The `workers` argument currently records a request but both binary and
clustered engines execute the serial reference path. It is therefore not a
speed claim, and objects with different requests are not byte-identical because
their computation metadata differs:

```{r verify-workers}
w1 <- bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 200, seed = 7, workers = 1, warn = FALSE)
w16 <- bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 200, seed = 7, workers = 16, warn = FALSE)
stopifnot(
  identical(w1$draws, w16$draws),
  identical(w16$computation$execution, "deterministic_serial_reference"),
  identical(w16$computation$workers_requested, 16L),
  !identical(w1, w16)
)
w16$computation[c("workers_requested", "execution")]
```

No draw-index prefix guarantee is claimed for the clustered generator. A real
parallel backend would require its own worker-count, execution-receipt, and
clustered-stream tests before the contract could be broadened.

## Hash provenance

Reproducing a number requires reproducing its **input**. The full digest is
`analysis_input_hash`:

```{r hashes}
p <- bm_provenance(fit)
p[c("analysis_input_hash", "row_hash", "item_set_hash",
    "score_map_hash", "support_hash", "cluster_id_hash")]
```

It hashes the complete scored response matrix, included row IDs, ordered item
names, normalized point weights, declared supports, and—when present—complete
cluster labels and the declared target. A one-cell response mutation therefore
changes it.

The narrower component hashes remain because they tell you where a mismatch
began:

| Component hash | Diagnoses |
|---|---|
| `row_hash` | which respondents entered, after missing-data filtering |
| `item_set_hash` | which items, in what order |
| `score_map_hash` | any recoding applied |
| `support_hash` | the declared response categories |
| `cluster_id_hash` | complete cluster membership and labels, when applicable |

A reader who reruns the code and matches `analysis_input_hash` has matched the
canonical analysis input. The component hashes help diagnose a mismatch but,
individually or together, are not a response-value digest.

Report the full hash with the seed, draw count, package version, and method ID.
That record identifies the computation; a fresh stochastic call is expected to
match exactly only when its RNG and execution contract also match.

## Monte Carlo diagnostics

The interval has two distinct sources of variability, and conflating them is
the usual mistake. **Sampling** variability is what the interval reports.
**Simulation** variability is the noise from using finitely many draws, and it
is a property of your compute budget rather than of your data.

```{r mc}
bm_mc_diagnostics(fit)
```

Read the endpoint standard errors against the precision you intend to report.
Reporting three decimals with simulation noise in the third is reporting noise.
Two further quantities check the same thing differently: the batch deviation
compares endpoints across independent batches, and the prefix-half difference
compares the first half of the draws with the whole.

```{r fig-stability, fig.alt = "Interval endpoints against cumulative draw count, both settling as draws accumulate."}
bm_plot_mc_stability(fit)
```

More draws shrink simulation noise. They do not shrink the interval, because
the interval is not about the simulation.

## Typed failures

Every refusal in this package raises a condition with a class, so failures can
be handled programmatically rather than by matching message text.

```{r conditions}
res <- tryCatch(
  bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 200, seed = 1, level = 0.90),
  bm_input_error = function(e) class(e)
)
res
```

```{r guardrails}
g <- bm_guardrails()
nrow(g)
g[1:3, c("situation", "reason")]
```

All `r nrow(bm_guardrails())` situations are listed with the reason and what to
do instead. The design principle behind them is worth stating plainly: **where
the software cannot know the answer, it fails rather than defaulting.**
`cluster_target` has no default because the two targets are different
questions. `supports` has no default because the denominator depends on it. The
historical two-stage interval refuses below 22 clusters because its shrinkage
was never confirmed there, and the default clustered interval reports on the
result whether its cluster count lies inside the confirmed range rather than
pretending the evidence extends. In each case a default would have been a
scientific choice made silently on the user's behalf.

## The validation record

**Binary path.** Two stages on the same 32 population laws in four families,
with undefined intervals counted as misses. The confirmatory stage (108,000
replications) met all 9 prespecified acceptance criteria; the calibrated
interval covered 94.5%–95.1% by family in the 22 regular cells. A paired
comparison on fresh samples then computed six standard intervals on each: the
calibrated interval covered 94.8% (families 94.5%–95.0%), 0.41 percentage
points more than the raw interval at a mean-length cost of 2.46%–2.65%; the
nonparametric-bootstrap BCa and percentile intervals covered 95.3% and 94.6%,
and the `mokken` delta-method Wald and range-preserving intervals 94.1% and
94.2%.

**Clustered path.** A fresh confirmation of 41,000 datasets on 24
conditions, 21 of them regular, crossing 22–320 clusters, balanced,
size-dependent and SWMDK-like cluster sizes, latent intraclass correlations
from 0 to .35, and three stress conditions at or near a population knot. The
adjusted complete-record interval covered .947 (respondent-weighted) and .949
(equal-cluster) over the regular conditions; the percentile interval of the
same draws .935 and .936; the two-stage law of version 0.9.0 .997 raw and
.977 after its shrinkage; the clustered delta interval .984. All four
prespecified criteria were established in 36 of 42 condition–target
assessments, every lower-tail and failure criterion among them.

The binary constant was selected on training conditions, evaluated once on
held-out conditions, and then confirmed prospectively. The clustered
multiplier $k_G$ is a prespecified function of the cluster count, chosen
between two prespecified candidates on development data, screened once on
validation data, and then confirmed. Both are frozen, and each coverage claim
attaches to that construction alone.

### The software's own checks

The binary article reports the test suite of the version that produced its
results, **665 unit tests** in package version 0.0.0.9001; the earlier version
of the clustered article reported **791 expectations across 24 files** in the
same package version, and the clustered article's current version computes its
results in its replication archive and names this package's coefficient kernel.
This release is larger, because the user-facing surface and the complete-record
path are themselves tested:

```{r test-scale, echo = FALSE}
data.frame(
  version = c("0.0.0.9001 (the articles' results)", "0.9.0 (previous release)",
              "0.10.0 (this release)"),
  scale   = c("665 tests / 791 expectations", "2,320 expectations across 42 files",
              "287 tests / 3,444 passing expectations across 51 files")
)
```

The 0.10.0 count is the public repository's verification run: 3,444
expectations passed and one gallery test was skipped because it requires
development-only renders (3,445 total testthat records). That gallery test
adds nine expectations when its development-only renders are available.

The numbers are not in conflict and a later one does not supersede an earlier
one: the articles' figures describe the version that computed the published
results, which is the version their claims rest on. For the current clustered
procedure that version is the archive, and this release's
`test-swmdk-reproduction.R` and the published-number gate tie the package to
it at the article's own seeds.

What connects the two is the parity gate. It compares eight fixtures field by
field against a reference produced by 0.0.0.9001 (numeric fields at `1e-12`;
seeds, policies and RNG settings exactly; two float-derived clustered digests
for presence only), subject to the five documented additive/corrected fields
named in `NEWS.md`. The
ordinary gate runner executes G-1 through G-10; G-10 installs the current source
into an isolated library and deep-compares every cached fit after removing only
its build date. The external paper-number gate is separate and opt-in with
`--published`; it is mandatory for a release receipt, not silently included in
an ordinary development run.

## Limits

Six, stated plainly.

**Item selection is not propagated.** The estimand is a declared, fixed scale.
If items were chosen by looking at these data, the interval is too narrow by an
amount not quantified here.

**The constructions are validated within lanes.** The binary correction was
confirmed for the scale coefficient of binary items; the clustered adjustment
for polytomous items in 22–320 clusters. Item- and pair-level intervals carry
no correction and say so in their `interval_calibration` column.

**Small $G$ is computable, not confirmed.** The clustered interval runs for
two or more clusters, because the arithmetic allows it, and records
`OUTSIDE_CONFIRMED_CLUSTER_COUNT` below 22 and above 320 because the evidence
stops there. Nothing in the confirmation says what the interval does with
five clusters. The historical two-stage lane refuses below 22 instead.

**Non-probability samples.** Everything here concerns repeated sampling from a
population. If the respondents were not sampled in a way that supports that
frame, the interval answers a question you may not be asking.

**The intervals are frequentist.** The Bayesian bootstrap is the computational
device. No posterior interpretation is available, and no probability statement
about $H$ is computed at any level.

**No verdicts.** The package reports no decision about whether a scale is
adequate. `bm_benchmark()` gives arithmetic relations to the conventional
landmarks and stops there, because adequacy depends on the instrument's
purpose.
